source.title: Non-Gaussianity Reveals Interpretable Directions in Language Models
source.authors: Si-Da Liu; Fei-Jiang Han; Sarah Wiegreffe; Fu-Rong Huang

page_placements.theme: Heavy-tailed activation or weight statistics single out distinct neurons

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether interpretation scores change when ICA components are evaluated on the tail containing their coherent pattern rather than an arbitrary signed tail, and analyzes failures of automated scoring. It refines the measurement claim rather than testing polysemanticity rates.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test vision neurons, superposition as a cause of polysemanticity, or whether most transformer neurons respond to unrelated contexts. Its Qwen3-32B neuron analysis measures lexical concentration among extreme activations, not the frequency of unrelated response patterns. The direct claim-version result is about measurement sensitivity: ICA sign/tail selection and automated explanation coverage affect interpretability evaluation.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version of the claim. Its main results concern ICA directions in the residual stream, not MLP neurons, so they do not measure neuron polysemanticity. These results cover tail-sign effects on automated interpretability, kurtosis–interpretability links and SAE comparisons. The sign-sensitivity and scoring-failure results resemble V7, but they concern a different unit (learned ICA directions) and an interpretability score, not whether neurons count as polysemantic. The only native-neuron analysis (100 Qwen3-32B layer-0 neurons) measures lexical concentration among extreme activations against kurtosis. It gives no share of neurons responding to unrelated inputs, no layer comparison and no cause. Zoom In is cited only in the introduction, and MLP neurons are discussed as a privileged basis. These findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right but incomplete. The central conclusion is that non-Gaussianity is a direct unsupervised signal for discovering interpretable residual-stream directions. ICA components found this way are human- and LLM-interpretable, and interpretability rises with kurtosis. They are competitive with public SAEs on reconstruction, sparse probing and targeted perturbation at far lower cost. Correcting ICA's arbitrary sign recovers much of a previously reported interpretability gap. The caveats about automated scoring missing sparse tails or rewarding dataset regularities are secondary points from the error analysis.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses GPU-parallel symmetric FastICA and non-Gaussianity-based tail selection, not the original sources’ neuron visualization or SoLU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability assessment changes with ICA sign/tail orientation. Automated scores also depend on whether the evaluation examples cover sparse semantic tails and whether dataset-specific regularities create shortcuts. The paper reports robustness checks across fitting budgets, corpora, and evaluator pipelines.

fits_no_version.finding: For ICA residual-stream directions, evaluating the arbitrary positive tail reproduces a low ICA-vs-SAE interpretability gap on Pythia 70M. Evaluating the skewness-selected tail recovers much of the gap, and this holds across corpora, fitting budgets and evaluators (Fig. 4, 27, 28).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated interpretability scores for learned directions depend strongly on which signed tail of the activation distribution is evaluated.

fits_no_version.finding: Automated explanation–prediction scores can miss sparse coherent tails: a component has κ=665, r=0.09 because the evaluation corpus never reaches its C/C++ preprocessor tail. Scores can also be inflated by positional dataset regularities (κ=0.76, r=0.50).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanation-scoring of directions is sensitive to tail coverage in the evaluation corpus and to dataset shortcuts.

fits_no_version.finding: In 100 Qwen3-32B layer-0 MLP neurons, excess kurtosis correlates with lexical concentration of extreme activations (ρs=0.55; Q1 45.8% vs Q4 80.8%). The highest-kurtosis neuron has mixed natural-language/code extremes, with one position giving 99.4% of its fourth moment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Excess kurtosis may help rank native neurons for inspection, but tail inspection is needed to tell coherent patterns from isolated extremes.

record.problems: The native-neuron analysis samples 100 neurons from only layer 0 of one model and the authors say direct quantification of neuron interpretability remains future work. Automated interpretability can miss rare coherent tails or be inflated by dataset-specific patterns. Several interpretability comparisons are presented as figures with plotted values rather than numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results omitted. Other paper results on reconstruction, probing, steering, and efficiency do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons.
No share of transformer MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts; the neuron analysis covers one layer of one model and measures lexical concentration only.
No test of superposition or capacity pressure as a cause.
No test of polysemanticity from initialization, regularization or noise.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
No test of whether neuron polysemanticity classification changes with the activation range examined or the explanation scoring. The analogous tail and scoring results concern ICA directions only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 'tested' status was rejected because every V7-linked row measures ICA components, not neurons, and an interpretability score, not polysemanticity status. Rows r1–r3 are essentially the study's method compared with an SAE baseline. No verdict labels are given. The neuron appendix is one layer of one model and is described by the authors as preliminary.

versions.untested_parts: No image-classifier neurons or vision-model responses are tested.
The native-neuron analysis samples one layer of Qwen3-32B and measures lexical concentration among extreme positions, not the share responding to unrelated tokens or contexts across layers.
No test of superposition or capacity pressure as a cause of polysemanticity.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
The paper compares ICA with SAE representations but does not test the share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings.
The paper does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons to test whether their apparently unrelated responses share one feature.
Tests ICA component tail orientation and automated interpretability scoring, not the full range of possible activation thresholds or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated ICA component interpretability using the arbitrary positive sign in the explanation–prediction pipeline.
rows.measure: Automated interpretability score (Pearson correlation between predicted and observed token-level scores)
rows.note: The text says this reproduces the previously reported ICA–SAE gap under arbitrary-sign evaluation. Figure values are plotted by layer.
rows.check: Measures automated interpretability of ICA residual-stream components (arbitrary sign) vs SAE features, not neurons. V7 concerns neurons. This is the study's comparison of its method with SAEs, and the value is figure-only.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the same fitted ICA axes using the skewness-selected, stronger tail.
rows.measure: Automated interpretability score (Pearson correlation between predicted and observed token-level scores)
rows.note: The text says correcting the sign recovers much of the gap and makes ICA competitive with SAE. Figure values are plotted by layer.
rows.check: Same as r1: the sign-corrected ICA component score is a method-vs-SAE comparison on directions, not neurons. It does not bear on V7 as worded.

rows.subject: Qwen 3.5 9B Base
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated ICA components on the skewness-selected, stronger tail.
rows.note: The text describes sign-corrected ICA as competitive with the public SAE baseline; the figure plots results by layer.
rows.check: ICA components in Qwen 3.5 9B vs public SAE; figure-only method comparison, not a neuron measurement.

rows.subject: Qwen 3.5 9B Base, L7/C338
rows.operation_detail: Compared the component's non-Gaussianity with automated explanation–prediction interpretability when evaluation examples covered its semantic tail.

conditions.value: selected examples reach the high-activation tail

rows.measure: Excess kurtosis and automated interpretability score
rows.value: excess kurtosis κ = 47.98; automated score r = 0.88
rows.note: The text describes this as agreement between a well-covered semantic tail and a high automated score.
rows.check: Single ICA component case study (kurtosis 47.98, r=0.88), illustrating agreement between metrics; not a neuron and not polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Qwen 3.5 9B Base, L7/C2035
rows.operation_detail: Compared non-Gaussianity with automated interpretability when the evaluation corpus failed to reach the component's sparse semantic tail.

conditions.value: OpenWebText evaluation fragments did not reach comparable tail activations

rows.measure: Excess kurtosis and automated interpretability score
rows.value: excess kurtosis κ = 665.34; automated score r = 0.09
rows.note: The text reports a coherent but very sparse C/C++ preprocessor tail that the sampled evaluation examples missed.
rows.check: ICA component case showing a tail-coverage failure of automated scoring. 'Partial' has no referent; this is not a neuron polysemanticity measure.

rows.subject: Qwen 3.5 9B Base, L15/C1503
rows.operation_detail: Compared non-Gaussianity with automated interpretability for a component whose evaluation examples contained a dataset-specific positional regularity.

conditions.value: position-0 regularity made examples predictable despite an inadequate initial lexical explanation

rows.measure: Excess kurtosis and automated interpretability score
rows.value: excess kurtosis κ = 0.76; automated score r = 0.50
rows.note: Controlled examples showed that unrelated position-0 tokens also activated, so the score reflected a positional pattern rather than the initial proposed lexical explanation.
rows.check: ICA component case showing a positional shortcut inflating the score. 'Partial' has no referent, and the unit is not a neuron.
